# Check The Scoreboard: An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation

Nishant Balepur Affiliation: University of Maryland Affiliation: New
York University Email: [nbalepur@umd.edu](mailto:)    Paiheng Xu
Affiliation: University of Maryland
Email: [jordan.ying@ntu.edu.sg](mailto:)    Wei Ai
Affiliation: University of Maryland    Eunsol Choi Affiliation: New York
University    Rachel Rudinger Affiliation: University of Maryland   
Jordan Boyd-Graber¹¹footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: Nanyang Technological
University

###### Abstract

Multiple-choice question answering (mcqa) benchmarks in nlp use
number-right scoring (accuracy), but in educational testing, the scoring
scheme—the combination of the response mode models follow and the rule
for grading responses—is a key design choice that dictates which
abilities to reward. We examine how alternatives to number right change
what mcqa measures with six education-inspired schemes that assess
abilities beyond accuracy: distractor elimination, abstention,
confidence calibration, and self-correction. On llm benchmarks, these
schemes: 1) shift rankings of 31 llms beyond rephrased number right
prompts; 2) better predict the llms users prefer in LLM Arena; and 3)
reveal distinct model capabilities, like that GPT-5 rarely abstains and
readily self-corrects, while weaker open-weight models often abstain and
hesitate to eliminate choices. Given the benefits of alternative scoring
schemes, we discuss ways to extend them to tasks beyond mcqa.²² 2 Our
code: https://github.com/nbalepur/mcqa-scoring/²²footnotetext: Work done
at University of Maryland

|                                                                     |                                            |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Name                                                                | Abilities Tested                           | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| Number Right ([Kelly, 1916](#bib.bib38), NR)                        | Answer Accuracy                            | The standard method where the model picks a best answer. +1 point if correct and 0 if incorrect.                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| Control Variation (NR-Var)                                          | Prompt Sensitivity                         | To set a baseline prompt sensitivity when testing different schemes, we rephrase the prompt of NR.                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| Negative Marking ([Holt, 2006](#bib.bib59), NM)                     | Uncertainty, Abstention                    | The model picks one best answer or abstains. To penalize guessing, scoring awards +1 point for right answers, $`-1/(n-1)`$ for wrong ones, and 0 for abstaining, so the expected value of guessing is 0.                                                                                                                       |
| Elimination Scoring ([Coombs et al., 1956](#bib.bib5), Elim)        | Partial Knowledge, Eliminative Reasoning   | The model picks as many answers it thinks are wrong. For granular partial knowledge, the score is the proportion of all distractors eliminated, or $`0`$ points if the correct answer is eliminated.                                                                                                                           |
| Elimination + NM ([Coombs et al., 1956](#bib.bib5), Elim-NM)        | Partial Know., Elim. Reasoning, Abstention | A scoring scheme that combines the benefits and abilities tested in Elim and NM: models receive $`1/(n-1)`$ points for eliminating wrong answers and $`-1`$ for correct ones.                                                                                                                                                  |
| Confidence-Based Marking ([Gardner-Medwin, 2006](#bib.bib16), CBM)  | Discrete Confidence Calibration            | The model predicts one answer choice and a confidence level ($`C=1`$ for low, $`C=2`$ for medium, or $`C=3`$ for high). To reward calibration, predicting $`C=1`$ yields $`+1`$ if correct and $`0`$ if wrong, $`C=2`$ yields $`+2`$ if correct and $`-2`$ if wrong, and $`C=3`$ yields $`+3`$ if correct and $`-6`$ if wrong. |
| Personal Point Allocation ([MacNeil et al., 2023](#bib.bib17), PPA) | Probabilistic Conf. Calibration            | The model outputs a probability distribution for each choice being correct. To reward confidently right answers, we use Brier score between the model’s distribution and the true distribution (one-hot).                                                                                                                      |
| Answer Until Correct ([Wilcox, 1982](#bib.bib18), AUC)              | Self-Correction, Adaptability              | Over a fixed number of tries, the model answers until correct—told when incorrect. To reward fewer attempts, the score is $`(r-1)/(n-1)`$, where $`r`$ is \# choices left when the correct answer is picked.                                                                                                                   |

## 1 Introduction: Keeping Score in mcqa

In multiple-choice question answering ([Clark et al., 2020](#bib.bib29),
mcqa) benchmarks, nlp researchers carefully study question and inference
design [Gu et al. (2025)](#bib.bib67), but stick to the simplest scoring
scheme of number right scoring: models receive one point for each
correct answer (i.e., accuracy). Despite longstanding concerns that this
rewards guessing ([Du et al., 2023](#bib.bib60)) and poorly reflects
abilities users value ([Saxon et al., 2024](#bib.bib73)), it persists
due to its simplicity.

Conversely, education research offers alternative schemes that punish
guessing, elicit confidence, or add re-attempts [Lau et al.
(2011)](#bib.bib58). These schemes surface student abilities that number
right scoring cannot distinguish [Kanzow et al. (2023)](#bib.bib23), but
add costs like test anxiety that limit adoption [Ndu et al.
(2016)](#bib.bib19). However, these schemes test abilities llms
lack—confidence, abstention, and self-correction—and llms do not
experience test anxiety [Shanahan (2024)](#bib.bib13), making nlp
well-positioned to adapt them.

Our paper presents six mcqa scoring schemes for llm evaluation that use
alternative prompt instructions and metrics
(Table [1](#S0.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation")).
Grounded in education research, our schemes assess how well llms abstain
when uncertain to avoid penalties, use partial knowledge to eliminate
distractors, express calibrated confidence in predictions, and
self-correct after being informed they are wrong—distinct abilities that
mcqa neglects with number right scoring.

Across 31 llms and three mcqa
datasets ([section 2](#S2 "2 Experimental Setup: Scoring Schemes ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation")),
many schemes shift llm ranks more than rephrasing instructions in our
number right prompt, testing unique
abilities ([section 3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Different Schemes, Different Ranks ‣ 3 Results: Analyzing Scoring Schemes ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation")).
Answer until correct scoring best predicts the llms that users prefer in
LLM Arena ([Zheng et al., 2024](#bib.bib44)), helping mcqa better
reflect what users value
([section 3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 AUC Agrees with Human Preferences ‣ 3 Results: Analyzing Scoring Schemes ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation")).
Our schemes also reveal llm behaviors: larger llms with test-time
reasoning are more consistent over schemes
([section 3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Capturing Cross-Scheme Contradictions ‣ 3 Results: Analyzing Scoring Schemes ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation")),
strong GPT-5 models rarely abstain and are quick to change answers,
Command-R+ often abstains, and LLaMA-3.1 hesitates to eliminate
incorrect choices
([section 3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Scoring Schemes Reveal Model Behaviors ‣ 3 Results: Analyzing Scoring Schemes ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation"))—quirks
that number right fails to surface.

These scoring schemes require only prompt and metric changes, making
them simple to incorporate into existing mcqa benchmarks. We
more broadly argue for the importance of scoring scheme design in
benchmarks and conclude with ways to extend them beyond mcqa
([section 5](#S5 "5 Conclusion: Scheming Beyond mcqa ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation")).
Our contributions are:

1. Six education-grounded scoring schemes, evaluated across three mcqa
   benchmarks and 31 llms.
2. Evidence that scoring schemes test diverse abilities and better
   predict model ranks in LLM Arena.
3. Cross-scheme analyses of consistency, measurements, confidence, and
   self-correction behaviors.

## 2 Experimental Setup: Scoring Schemes

Drawing on [Koele et al. (1987)](#bib.bib56), a scoring scheme combines
a response mode (how test-takers must respond to inputs) and a scoring
rule (how to score responses). Practically in llm evaluation, prompts
define response modes (e.g., “Select the correct answer”) and metrics
(e.g., accuracy) dictate scoring.

mcqa’s default scoring scheme is number right ([Kelly,
1916](#bib.bib38), NR): given a question $`q`$ and $`n`$ choices
$`\mathcal{C}`$, test-takers predict one answer
$`\hat{a}\in\mathcal{C}`$—the response mode. The scoring rule assigns
one point if $`\hat{a}`$ matches the gold answer
($`\mathds{1}(a=\hat{a})`$). Despite its popularity, NR cannot
distinguish lucky guesses from true understanding and provides no credit
for test-takers’ partial knowledge [Lau et al. (2011)](#bib.bib58),
which also applies to nlp models ([Du et al., 2023](#bib.bib60)).

To see whether alternative scoring schemes can bolster llm evaluation,
we study mcqa schemes inspired by education
(Table [1](#S0.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation")):
negative marking (NM) to penalize guessing [Frary (1988)](#bib.bib40),
answer elimination (Elim, Elim-NM) for partial credit based on the
number of ruled-out choices [Coombs et al. (1956)](#bib.bib5),
confidence elicitation (CBM, PPA) to reward calibrated certainty [de
Finetti (1965)](#bib.bib41), and answering until correct (AUC) to
evaluate how test-takers adapt to feedback [Wilcox (1982)](#bib.bib18).
These test desired abilities of llms that NR cannot capture [Liang et
al. (2023)](#bib.bib55)—abstention [Elhady et al. (2025)](#bib.bib36),
eliminative reasoning [Ma and Du (2023)](#bib.bib46), calibration [Guo
et al. (2017)](#bib.bib70), and self-correction [Huang et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib48)—valuable additions to mcqa.

We implement each scheme via custom prompts outlining response modes,
and metrics as scoring rules. To illustrate, for NM, we adapt NR’s
prompt to let llms abstain as part of the response mode, and the scoring
rule to add penalties for wrong answers
(Table [1](#S0.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation"),
row 3). We repeat this process for each row in Table
[1](#S0.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation")—prompting
llms to return wrong choices in a list for Elim/Elim-NM, predictions
with confidence scores in CBM/PPA, and add past predictions as inputs
for AUC—specified in
Appendix [A.7](#A1.SS7 "A.7 Prompts ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation").
All prompts use mcqa templates drawn from the InspectAI library [UK AISI
(2024)](#bib.bib53).

### 2.1 Datasets

We sample $`1000`$ mcqs from three popular benchmarks of varied
difficulty: 1) ARC–grade-school scientific knowledge/commonsense [Clark
et al. (2018)](#bib.bib42); 2) MMLU—knowledge of 57 college topics
[Hendrycks et al. (2021)](#bib.bib43); and 3) SuperGPQA—knowledge of 285
graduate topics [Du et al. (2025)](#bib.bib35).

### 2.2 Models

We assess 31 frontier llms: 1) Gemini ([Comanici et al.,
2025](#bib.bib65), 2/3 Flash, 2.5 Lite, 2.5/3 Pro); 2) GPT ([Singh et
al., 2025](#bib.bib1), 4.1, 5 Nano, 5 Mini, 5, 5.2); 3) Claude
([Anthropic, 2025](#bib.bib64), 3.7/4/4.5 Sonnet, 4.5 Haiku); 4) Cohere
Command-R ([Gomez, 2024](#bib.bib63), R, R+, R7B); 5) DeepSeek ([Guo et
al., 2025](#bib.bib34), V3.1, R1); 6) Qwen-3 ([Yang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib61), 80B Inst/Think, 235B Inst/Think); 7) LLaMA-3.1
([Dubey et al., 2024](#bib.bib62), 8B, 70B, 405B); 8) GPT OSS ([Agarwal
et al., 2025](#bib.bib20), 20B, 120B); 9) GLM ([Zeng et al.,
2025](#bib.bib21), 4.5, 4.6); and 10) Kimi-K2 [Team et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib22). GPT-OSS and Cmd-R+ take a week on SuperGPQA, so we
omit them. We use default model parameters.

## 3 Results: Analyzing Scoring Schemes

Having designed education-based mcqa schemes
([section 2](#S2 "2 Experimental Setup: Scoring Schemes ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation")),
we now reveal their benefits for nlp: they reward new abilities
([section 3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Different Schemes, Different Ranks ‣ 3 Results: Analyzing Scoring Schemes ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation")),
predict user preferences
([section 3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 AUC Agrees with Human Preferences ‣ 3 Results: Analyzing Scoring Schemes ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation")),
and surface model behaviors
([section 3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Capturing Cross-Scheme Contradictions ‣ 3 Results: Analyzing Scoring Schemes ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation"),
[section 3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Scoring Schemes Reveal Model Behaviors ‣ 3 Results: Analyzing Scoring Schemes ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation")).

### 3.1 Different Schemes, Different Ranks

While our alternative scoring schemes differ from NR by design, we do
not need them if they measure the same model abilities as NR, as their
adoption would never impact downstream evaluation [Cronbach and Meehl
(1955)](#bib.bib72). To probe this, we measure the Spearman’s
correlation between llm rankings under each scheme versus NR. Low
correlation indicates discriminant validity [Campbell and Fiske
(1959)](#bib.bib12): the scheme evaluates abilities NR does not.

NM and CBM have high rank correlation with NR
(Fig [1](#S3.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 3.1 Different Schemes, Different Ranks ‣ 3 Results: Analyzing Scoring Schemes ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation")),
but Elim, Elim-NM, PPA, and AUC consistently show lower correlation
than the NR-Var control, testing skills NR does not capture beyond
rephrased instructions. This trend also holds on ARC when shuffling
choices and replacing letters with numbers (e.g., (A) $`\rightarrow`$
(1)) as sensitivity baselines in Appendix
Table [2](#A1.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Answer Until Correct (AUC, Prompt ). ‣ A.7 Prompts ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation").
There is not a best scheme, as this depends on what researchers value:
Elim for eliminative reasoning, PPA for calibration, and AUC for
self-correction
(Table [1](#S0.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation")).
NR cannot target such skills, which have downstream use: medical
chatbots apply Elim in diagnosis by exclusion [Fred (2013)](#bib.bib27),
while ai tutors apply AUC when adapting to student errors [Chen et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib26).

### 3.2 AUC Agrees with Human Preferences

While user feedback is the north-star goal for llm development ([Ouyang
et al., 2022](#bib.bib52)), researchers often rely on cheaper offline
proxies such as mcqa to guide training [Olmo et al. (2025)](#bib.bib11).
To test whether alternative scoring schemes improve mcqa as an online
proxy, we compare llm ranks under each scheme to LLM Arena ranks—a
large-scale benchmark of user preferences via live voting
that developers actively optimize for [Spangher et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib10).

AUC best agrees with LLM Arena
(Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.1 Different Schemes, Different Ranks ‣ 3 Results: Analyzing Scoring Schemes ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation"))—more
than NR—so AUC can better predict llms users prefer pre-deployment. This
matches [Shi et al. (2024)](#bib.bib15) and [Liu et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib14) who show users prefer llms that adapt well to
feedback, which AUC captures by making llms self-correct; this trend
holds in a scheme where llms always self-reflect
(Appendix [A.4](#A1.SS4 "A.4 Full LLM Arena Analysis ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation")).
As expected, the gap between NR’s and AUC’s correlation with LLM Arena
is wider on technical queries (e.g., Math, Expert) versus those
unrelated to mcqa (e.g., Creative Writing).

### 3.3 Capturing Cross-Scheme Contradictions

We now show alternative scoring schemes’ value in tracking logical
consistency [Hase et al. (2023)](#bib.bib7): a model should not
contradict its belief of the answer across schemes [Chern et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib4). We test consistency in two ways: 1) the answer a
model picks in NR must not be eliminated in Elim; and 2) NR’s answer
must have the most weight in PPA (or tied).

Figure
[3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3.1 Different Schemes, Different Ranks ‣ 3 Results: Analyzing Scoring Schemes ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation")
shows that for llms of the same family, scaling parameters or adding
test-time reasoning improves consistency, aligning with prior work
[Truong et al. (2023)](#bib.bib24). Thus, running diverse scoring
schemes for the same task like mcqa is a simple way to evaluate which
interventions (e.g., scaling size or inference) can improve model
consistency.

### 3.4 Scoring Schemes Reveal Model Behaviors

While NR mainly provides just one accuracy score to study models,
alternative schemes also give finer-grained signals into model behavior,
like abstention rates, confidence, and adaptability
(Figure [4](#S3.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 3.1 Different Schemes, Different Ranks ‣ 3 Results: Analyzing Scoring Schemes ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation")).
Analyzing this yields interesting trends: 1) GPT models rarely abstain
and state high confidence; 2) weak GPT models struggle to change answers
after being told they are incorrect, while stronger GPT models readily
do so; 3) weaker open-weight models like Command-R+ and Llama often
abstain or hesitate to eliminate choices; and 4) All llms state high
confidence in CBM and rarely abstain in NM on easier datasets like ARC
and MMLU, but not Super GPQA, showing some awareness of mcq difficulty
[Guo et al. (2017)](#bib.bib70). Only evaluating mcqa via NR scoring
obscures these features of llm behavior.

## 4 Related Work

Scoring Schemes: mcqa exams originally tested students via number right
scoring [Kelly (1916)](#bib.bib38), but educators found limitations: it
encourages students to guess when unsure [Guilford
(1936)](#bib.bib25) and cannot discern partial knowledge if
students answer identically [Lau et al. (2011)](#bib.bib58). Educators
have thus designed alternatives schemes to improve abilities mcqa
measures [Cronbach and Meehl (1955)](#bib.bib72), so we extend them and
assess their benefits in nlp.

mcqa Evaluation: mcqa is a keystone of nlp evaluation [Reddy
(1988)](#bib.bib47) as it is simple and mirrors student testing [Clark
et al. (2020)](#bib.bib29). Given this dominance [Liang et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib55), work improves the task via open-ended formats
[Myrzakhan et al. (2024)](#bib.bib71); [Chandak et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib37), shortcut reduction [Balepur and Rudinger
(2024)](#bib.bib68); [Balepur et al. (2026a)](#bib.bib33), and quality
control [Moore et al. (2024)](#bib.bib66); [Palta et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib49); [Balepur et al. (2026c)](#bib.bib32). Some of our
mcqa schemes have been studied individually: [Ma and Du
(2023)](#bib.bib46) and [Balepur et al. (2024a)](#bib.bib57) test
process of elimination, [Elhady et al. (2025)](#bib.bib36) add an “I
don’t know” option for abstention, and [Huang et al. (2024)](#bib.bib48)
assess self-correction. We instead compare schemes from education to
study rank shifts, preference agreement, and behaviors. Work also
studies how scoring can better adapt training and evaluation curricula
([Hofmann et al., 2025](#bib.bib51); [Meng et al., 2026](#bib.bib39),
e.g., Item Response Theory), but our scoring schemes focus on evaluating
individual examples.

## 5 Conclusion: Scheming Beyond mcqa

nlp often critiques mcqa since models can guess [Du et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib60); [Balepur et al. (2024b)](#bib.bib50) and the task
poorly reflects downstream user needs [Saxon et al. (2024)](#bib.bib73);
[Balepur et al. (2025)](#bib.bib54), but it persists due to its
simplicity. Educators face similar issues when testing students, so they
design alternative scoring schemes. nlp can take the same path: easy
fixes to prompts and metrics can curb guessing by design, reveal
distinct model behaviors, and better predict user preferences, all
without changing task inputs.

More broadly, we argue for human assessments to inform llm scoring
scheme design. In mcqa, we use educational testing, which also applies
to programming [White (1993)](#bib.bib2) and writing [Tew and Guzdial
(2010)](#bib.bib3) which have well-researched scoring rubrics and
assignment creation protocols for students [Roumani (2002)](#bib.bib6).
For nlp tasks sans human analogues ([Bragg et al., 2025](#bib.bib28);
[Balepur et al., 2026b](#bib.bib31), e.g., deep research), a promising
path is to study how humans finish them and which behaviors predict
success. Lastly, the benefits of AUC’s multi-turn setting with simulated
user feedback suggests that more classic nlp tasks (e.g., natural
language inference, summarization) could be run as multi-turn dialogues,
forming user-inspired evaluations [Pan et al. (2025)](#bib.bib9); [Laban
et al. (2026)](#bib.bib30). Overall, researchers must treat scoring
schemes as a key part of benchmark construction, just like educators do.

## 6 Limitations

llms are sensitive to prompting formats, especially in mcqa [Pezeshkpour
and Hruschka (2024)](#bib.bib45), so altering prompts could shift model
ranks further [Alzahrani et al. (2024)](#bib.bib69). To design prompts
fairly, we build off the mcqa prompts used in InspectAI [UK AISI
(2024)](#bib.bib53): a standard evaluation framework from the United
Kingdom AI Security Institute. This also applies to our analysis with
LLM Arena [Zheng et al. (2023)](#bib.bib74), as the platform does not
disclose the prompts or inference parameters used, so different
configurations could alter our results. Prompt sensitivity is another
interesting aspect of llm evaluation that future work can explore when
considering alternative scoring schemes.

Second, while Answer Until Correct (AUC) is the scoring strategy with
the highest agreement with LLM Arena, it is the most expensive, as it
requires many turns (cost in
Table [3](#A1.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Answer Until Correct (AUC, Prompt ). ‣ A.7 Prompts ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation")).
While still cheaper than crowdsourcing, future work could test alternate
ways to reap the benefits of AUC with less attempts: in
Appendix [A.4](#A1.SS4 "A.4 Full LLM Arena Analysis ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation"),
we show prompting llms to self-refine their answers just once improves
agreement with LLM Arena. However, our goal is not to argue for a
particular mcqa scoring scheme, but to motivate the benefits of
evaluating with different scoring schemes, regardless of task.

## 7 Ethical Considerations

Our goal of testing different multiple-choice scoring regimes is to
improve evaluation validity, but we never intend to argue that such
evaluations are sufficient as pre-deployment checks. Models that excel
in our schemes may still be prone to biases, hallucinations, and
producing harmful outputs.

Generative AI (GenAI) was used in this project. We used Cursor³³ 3
https://cursor.com/agents to design plots, refactor code, and debug
errors, and we used ChatGPT to refine paper writing for brevity. AI
tools did not directly write any parts of this paper. We take full
responsibility for any GenAI errors. By discussing AI usage here, we
encourage other researchers to do the same.

## Appendix A Appendix

### A.1 Dataset Details

We select $`1000`$ random examples from the testing splits of ARC [Clark
et al. (2018)](#bib.bib42), MMLU [Hendrycks et al. (2021)](#bib.bib43),
and Super GPQA [Du et al. (2025)](#bib.bib35). All datasets are publicly
available, so our experiments are within their intended use. We did not
collect any datasets, so we did not check for PII. To our knowledge, all
questions are in English.

### A.2 Experiment Details

We implement all llms in InspectAI via LiteLLM⁴⁴ 4
https://docs.litellm.ai/. We access all closed-source llms via their
native APIs (e.g. the OpenAI API for GPT-5). For open-weight llms, we
use the Cohere API⁵⁵ 5 https://cohere.com/ for Cohere models and
TogetherAI⁶⁶ 6 https://www.together.ai/ for the rest. We allocate 24 CPU
hours for each experiment. All results are reported from one run. The
model endpoints are:

[7](#A1.T7 "Table 7 ‣ Answer Until Correct (AUC, Prompt ). ‣ A.7 Prompts ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation"),
and
[9](#A1.T9 "Table 9 ‣ Answer Until Correct (AUC, Prompt ). ‣ A.7 Prompts ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation")
have the llm scores of these rankings, respectively. To break ties in
ranks, we use Standard Competition or ‘‘1224’’ ranking,⁷⁷ 7
[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ranking#Standard_competition_ranking\_("1224"\_ranking)](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ranking#Standard_competition_ranking_(%221224%22_ranking)>)
where tied models share the same rank and ensuing positions are skipped
accordingly (e.g., 1, 2, 2, 4). GPT-5 is consistently the strongest
across datasets and scoring regimes—ranking the highest overall.

On SuperGPQA, Command-R+ and the GPT-OSS models timed out after 24 hours
under AUC scoring. Based on their current progress, we estimated that
these models would need up to a week to finish, so we did not re-run
them, and omitted them from any analysis that involved SuperGPQA.

We also evaluate Pearson’s correlation between scores directly (instead
of ranks) in
Figure [6](#A1.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Answer Until Correct (AUC, Prompt ). ‣ A.7 Prompts ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation")
which shows the same trend as
[section 3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Different Schemes, Different Ranks ‣ 3 Results: Analyzing Scoring Schemes ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation"):
schemes like Elim, PPA, and AUC reward behaviors distinct from NR.

### A.4 Full LLM Arena Analysis

Figure [7](#A1.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ Answer Until Correct (AUC, Prompt ). ‣ A.7 Prompts ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation")
shows the correlation between rankings for each scoring strategy and
prompt type in LLM Arena across all datasets. The trend in
[section 3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 AUC Agrees with Human Preferences ‣ 3 Results: Analyzing Scoring Schemes ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation")
holds over each dataset: the Answer Until Correct regime best correlates
with preferences from LLM Arena.

To understand the higher agreement from LLM Arena further, we design an
extension of AUC that executes two steps: 1) the model makes an initial
prediction; and 2) the model reflects on its answer and decide whether
it was correct or incorrect—following self-refine [Madaan et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib8). We run this scheme on ARC with GPT and open-weight
models in
[section 2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Models ‣ 2 Experimental Setup: Scoring Schemes ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation").
The self-refine ablation reaches an agreement of $`0.89`$, AUC reaches
$`0.86`$, and NR only reaches $`0.79`$—further indicating that the
ability to critically self-reflect is the behavior that correlates well
with human preferences.

### A.6 Full Model Behavior Analysis

Figures [16](#A1.F16 "Figure 16 ‣ Answer Until Correct (AUC, Prompt ). ‣ A.7 Prompts ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation"),
[17](#A1.F17 "Figure 17 ‣ Answer Until Correct (AUC, Prompt ). ‣ A.7 Prompts ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation"),
and
[18](#A1.F18 "Figure 18 ‣ Answer Until Correct (AUC, Prompt ). ‣ A.7 Prompts ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation")
show the behavioral analysis from
[section 3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Scoring Schemes Reveal Model Behaviors ‣ 3 Results: Analyzing Scoring Schemes ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation")
across all datasets, models, and evaluated scoring regimes.
Tables [5](#A1.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Answer Until Correct (AUC, Prompt ). ‣ A.7 Prompts ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation"),
[7](#A1.T7 "Table 7 ‣ Answer Until Correct (AUC, Prompt ). ‣ A.7 Prompts ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation"),
and
[9](#A1.T9 "Table 9 ‣ Answer Until Correct (AUC, Prompt ). ‣ A.7 Prompts ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation")
have the llm scores of these rankings, respectively.

#### GPT models rarely abstain and state high confidence.

Ranking models by NM abstention rate in
Figures [16](#A1.F16 "Figure 16 ‣ Answer Until Correct (AUC, Prompt ). ‣ A.7 Prompts ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation")
and [17](#A1.F17 "Figure 17 ‣ Answer Until Correct (AUC, Prompt ). ‣ A.7 Prompts ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation"),
GPT models occupy six of the ten lowest-abstaining positions; on the
harder Super GPQA
(Figure [18](#A1.F18 "Figure 18 ‣ Answer Until Correct (AUC, Prompt ). ‣ A.7 Prompts ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation")),
six of the eight least-abstaining models are GPT variants. An exception
is GPT-OSS-20B, a weaker open-sourced GPT model that falls near the
upper half of the abstention ranking across all datasets. GPT models
state high confidence as well: while most llms avoid low-confidence
responses on easier datasets like ARC and MMLU, GPT models take the six
positions with the fewest low-confidence responses on the harder Super
GPQA
(Figure [18](#A1.F18 "Figure 18 ‣ Answer Until Correct (AUC, Prompt ). ‣ A.7 Prompts ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation")).

#### Stronger GPT models readily revise answers after feedback; weaker ones struggle to do so.

The answer-change behavior from the figures supports this directly:
GPT-4.1, GPT-5, GPT-5.2, and GPT-OSS-120B fill four of the top six
answer-change positions on ARC
(Figure [16](#A1.F16 "Figure 16 ‣ Answer Until Correct (AUC, Prompt ). ‣ A.7 Prompts ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation"))
and all four of the top four on MMLU
(Figure [17](#A1.F17 "Figure 17 ‣ Answer Until Correct (AUC, Prompt ). ‣ A.7 Prompts ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation")).
On Super GPQA, GPT-OSS-120B exceeded our time budget, yet the other
three stronger GPT models still claim the top three positions
(Figure [18](#A1.F18 "Figure 18 ‣ Answer Until Correct (AUC, Prompt ). ‣ A.7 Prompts ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation")).
By contrast, GPT-5 Nano finishes last on ARC and second-to-last on Super
GPQA in answer-change rate, and GPT-5 Mini ranks near the bottom on ARC
and MMLU—the smallest GPT models are far less willing to revise answers
upon feedback.

#### Weaker open-weight models often abstain or hesitate to eliminate choices.

Command-R+ holds the single highest NM abstention rate on all three
datasets
(Figures [16](#A1.F16 "Figure 16 ‣ Answer Until Correct (AUC, Prompt ). ‣ A.7 Prompts ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation")–[18](#A1.F18 "Figure 18 ‣ Answer Until Correct (AUC, Prompt ). ‣ A.7 Prompts ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation")),
consistently the most likely model to pass rather than commit to an
answer. Llama models show the same avoidance tendency, but in Elim
rather than abstention: across all three datasets, Llama 3.1 70B ranks
last (31st on ARC and MMLU, 29th on Super GPQA), Llama 3.1 8B remains
near the bottom (29th on ARC and MMLU, 28th on Super GPQA), and even
Llama 3.1 405B falls in the lower quarter (24th–25th on ARC and MMLU,
23rd on Super GPQA)—indicating a systematic reluctance to rule out
incorrect options for Llama models.

#### All llms show high confidence and low abstention on easier datasets, but not on Super GPQA.

On ARC and MMLU, most models predominantly express high confidence and
rarely abstain. On Super GPQA this changes markedly: abstention rates
rise and models that predominantly expressed high confidence on easier
tasks shift toward low and mid confidence
(Figures [16](#A1.F16 "Figure 16 ‣ Answer Until Correct (AUC, Prompt ). ‣ A.7 Prompts ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation")–[18](#A1.F18 "Figure 18 ‣ Answer Until Correct (AUC, Prompt ). ‣ A.7 Prompts ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation")).
Even the Elim elimination rates decline with difficulty, as models
eliminate fewer choices on harder questions.

### A.7 Prompts

We show the prompts for all eight scoring schemes in
Prompts [A.7](#A1.SS7.SSS0.Px8 "Answer Until Correct (AUC, Prompt ). ‣ A.7 Prompts ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation")–[A.7](#A1.SS7.SSS0.Px8 "Answer Until Correct (AUC, Prompt ). ‣ A.7 Prompts ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation").
Each scheme adapts the base NR prompt
(Prompt [A.7](#A1.SS7.SSS0.Px8 "Answer Until Correct (AUC, Prompt ). ‣ A.7 Prompts ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation"))—initially
drawn from InspectAI [UK AISI (2024)](#bib.bib53)—to alter the response
mode: how the llm responds to the mcq. Afterwards, the scheme may also
adjust the scoring rule via custom metrics.

#### Number Right (NR, Prompt [A.7](#A1.SS7.SSS0.Px8 "Answer Until Correct (AUC, Prompt ). ‣ A.7 Prompts ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation")).

This is the standard prompt used in mcqa: the response mode asks the
model to select one answer letter, and the scoring rule rewards only
correct answers ([Kelly, 1916](#bib.bib38)).

#### Control Variation (NR-Var, Prompt [A.7](#A1.SS7.SSS0.Px8 "Answer Until Correct (AUC, Prompt ). ‣ A.7 Prompts ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation")).

We rephrase NR’s task instruction with synonymous language while leaving
both the response mode and scoring rule unchanged, to isolate
sensitivity to prompt wording ([Alzahrani et al., 2024](#bib.bib69)).

#### Negative Marking (NM, Prompt [A.7](#A1.SS7.SSS0.Px8 "Answer Until Correct (AUC, Prompt ). ‣ A.7 Prompts ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation")).

We adapt NR’s response mode to let llms abstain (via ABSTAIN in the
answer field), and update the scoring rule to penalize wrong answers
while rewarding abstaining over guessing ([Holt, 2006](#bib.bib59)).

#### Elimination (Elim, Prompt [A.7](#A1.SS7.SSS0.Px8 "Answer Until Correct (AUC, Prompt ). ‣ A.7 Prompts ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation")).

Instead of selecting a correct answer, llms output a list of choices
they believe are wrong. The scoring rule is updated to grant partial
credit for each eliminated distractor, but revokes all credit if the
correct answer is eliminated ([Coombs et al., 1956](#bib.bib5)).

#### Elimination with Negative Marking (Elim-NM, Prompt [A.7](#A1.SS7.SSS0.Px8 "Answer Until Correct (AUC, Prompt ). ‣ A.7 Prompts ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation")).

We keep Elim’s elimination response mode but adapt the scoring rule to
additionally penalize eliminating the correct answer, combining
partial-knowledge credit with a guessing deterrent ([Coombs et al.,
1956](#bib.bib5)).

#### Confidence-Based Marking (CBM, Prompt [A.7](#A1.SS7.SSS0.Px8 "Answer Until Correct (AUC, Prompt ). ‣ A.7 Prompts ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation")).

We extend NR’s response mode to require a discrete confidence level
alongside the answer, and update the scoring rule so that higher
declared confidence amplifies both the reward for correct answers and
the penalty for wrong ones ([Gardner-Medwin, 2006](#bib.bib16)).

#### Personal Point Allocation (PPA, Prompt [A.7](#A1.SS7.SSS0.Px8 "Answer Until Correct (AUC, Prompt ). ‣ A.7 Prompts ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation")).

We replace NR’s single-answer response mode with a probability
distribution over all choices, and replace the binary scoring rule with
the Brier score to reward both accuracy and calibration ([MacNeil et
al., 2023](#bib.bib17)).

#### Answer Until Correct (AUC, Prompt [A.7](#A1.SS7.SSS0.Px8 "Answer Until Correct (AUC, Prompt ). ‣ A.7 Prompts ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Check The Scoreboard:An Analysis of Scoring Schemes on Multiple-Choice Evaluation")).

We adapt NR’s response mode to allow multiple attempts, injecting a
feedback block after each wrong answer that lists the llm’s prior
incorrect choices, and update the scoring rule to reward answering
correctly in fewer attempts ([Wilcox, 1982](#bib.bib18)).

datasets. We run Min-Max normalization on all scores. When considering
disagreements at the score level, the trends in

disagreements from NR, further suggesting that they test different
abilities.
